hints: Look at what changes in stage 1: the $\text{OH}$ of the $\text{COOH}$ group is replaced by $\text{Cl}$ to give $\text{COCl}$, think which type of reagent replaces $\text{OH}$ with $\text{Cl}$ without touching the benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Spot the functional group change**
You start with $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ and you make $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCl}$. Only the $\text{OH}$ part of the carboxylic acid has changed. The benzene ring and the $\text{CH}_{2}$ are untouched, so you need a chlorinating agent specific for $\text{COOH}$ to $\text{COCl}$.

Recall the three standard reagents**
Three reagents do exactly this job at A Level: phosphorus(V) chloride $\text{PCl}_{5}$, phosphorus(III) chloride $\text{PCl}_{3}$, and thionyl chloride $\text{SOCl}_{2}$. Any one of these is accepted here.
Final answer: $\text{PCl}_{5}$ or $\text{PCl}_{3}$ or $\text{SOCl}_{2}$

hints: Focus on the new linkage in S: a $\text{C=O}$ directly attached to $\text{N}$, think what family contains the $\text{CONH}$ unit.
walkthrough:
Read the new group in S**
In S you have $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. The carbonyl carbon is now bonded to nitrogen. That $\text{C(=O)N}$ arrangement is the defining feature to name.

Name it correctly**
A $\text{C(=O)N}$ group is an amide. Because the nitrogen also carries one ethyl group and one H, it is a secondary amide, but the word amide alone earns the mark.
Final answer: amide (secondary amide / N-substituted amide)

hints: Balance atoms between R plus $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}$ and S, the $\text{Cl}$ from $\text{COCl}$ and one $\text{H}$ from the amine must go somewhere.
walkthrough:
Track the atoms that are lost**
R provides $\text{COCl}$ and ethylamine provides $\text{H}$ on nitrogen. When the $\text{C-N}$ bond forms, $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{H}$ are expelled together as $\text{HCl}$.

Allow for the basic conditions**
In practice excess ethylamine acts as a base and neutralises that $\text{HCl}$ to give the salt $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-}$. Cambridge accepts either $\text{HCl}$ or ethylammonium chloride as the other product.
Final answer: $\text{HCl}$ / hydrogen chloride or $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{3}\text{Cl}$ / ethylammonium chloride

hints: Compare S and T: the $\text{C=O}$ of the amide becomes $\text{CH}_{2}$ in the amine, think which powerful hydride reagent is needed to reduce $\text{C=O}$ in an amide, as $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is too weak.
walkthrough:
See what is reduced**
S contains $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and T contains $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. The carbonyl oxygen is removed and replaced by two hydrogens, but the rest of the molecule is unchanged.

Choose the reagent that can do it**
Amides are very resistant to reduction. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ will not touch them. You need lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$, in dry ether followed by acid work up, which reduces the amide carbonyl all the way to $\text{CH}_{2}$ to give the amine.

hints: Think in terms of oxygen and hydrogen balance: oxygen is lost and hydrogen is gained when $\text{CONH}$ becomes $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}$.
walkthrough:
Apply the hydrogen and oxygen test**
Going from $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}$ you lose oxygen and gain hydrogen. Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen is reduction.

Confirm the type**
No C-C bond is broken and no new functional class other than amine is made by reduction, so the reaction type is simply reduction.

hints: Write the formula of ethylamine ($\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}$) and recall that the M+1 peak is almost entirely due to one $^{13}\text{C}$ (1.1% natural abundance per carbon atom), think how many carbons can contribute.
walkthrough:
Set up the isotope logic**
Ethylamine is $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{7}\text{N}$. Each carbon has a 1.1% chance of being $^{13}\text{C}$. With 2 carbons, the probability of M+1 is $2 \times 1.1\%$.

Scale to the size of the M peak**
The M peak itself has abundance 62, so:
$$ \text{abundance of M+1} = \frac{2 \times 1.1}{100} \times 62 = 1.364 $$
This gives about $1.36$ to $1.4$. Contributions from $^{2}\text{H}$ and $^{15}\text{N}$ are negligible at this level.
Final answer: relative abundance = $2 \times 1.1 \times 0.62 = 1.36$ (accept 1.4, min 2 s.f.)

hints: For m/e 29, look at the ethyl side of T ($\text{NHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$), what simple alkyl cation has mass $12 \times 2 + 5 = 29$?
For m/e 91, recall the very stable fragment formed by phenyl compounds with a $\text{CH}_{2}$ attached to the ring, what is the mass of $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$?
walkthrough:
Assign m/e 29**
Compound T is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. Cleavage of the $\text{N-CH}_{2}$ bond can release the ethyl group as a cation:
$$ \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}^{+} $$
Mass = $(2 \times 12) + 5 = 29$, exactly matching the peak.

Assign m/e 91**
Cleavage at the benzylic position gives the very stable benzyl cation:
$$ \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}^{+} $$
Mass = $(7 \times 12) + 7 = 91$. This ion is stabilised by delocalisation into the ring and is a classic peak for compounds containing $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}$.

Final answer: m/e 29: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$ / $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}^{+}$
m/e 91: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$ ($\text{[C}_{7}\text{H}_{7}\text{]}^{+}$ benzyl cation)

hints: Recall which type of proton appears well downfield near $\delta$ 7, think about the effect of the benzene ring current on protons attached directly to the ring.
walkthrough:
Use the chemical shift chart**
Protons on a benzene ring are strongly deshielded and appear at $\delta$ 6.0 to 9.0, typically around 7. Only protons labelled a are directly on the aromatic ring, so only a falls in this range. All alkyl and N-H protons appear below $\delta$ 4.

hints: Remember that $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ shakes remove peaks due to $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{N-H}$ protons that can exchange with deuterium, look for the proton on nitrogen in T.
walkthrough:
Find the exchangeable proton**
Proton d is the $\text{N-H}$ proton. It is labile and exchanges with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$:
$$ \text{N-H} + \text{D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{N-D} + \text{HOD} $$
Deuterium does not show in the $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR spectrum, so the peak for d disappears. C-H protons do not exchange.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule ignoring proton d (it does not split), a triplet means the proton has exactly two equivalent neighbours on the adjacent carbon.
walkthrough:
Apply n+1 without d**
You are told d does not split c or e. So count only C-H neighbours.
Proton b ($\text{PhCH}_{2}$) is next to $\text{CH}_{2}$(c) with 2 H, so $2+1 = 3$, triplet.
Proton c ($\text{CH}_{2}$N) is next to $\text{CH}_{2}$(b) with 2 H, so triplet.
Proton f ($\text{CH}_{3}$) is next to $\text{CH}_{2}$(e) with 2 H, so triplet.

Exclude the others**
Proton e ($\text{NCH}_{2}$) is next to $\text{CH}_{3}$(f) with 3 H, so it is a quartet, not a triplet. Proton a has complex aromatic splitting and d is a singlet that exchanges. Hence b, c and f only.
Final answer: b, c, f

hints: Lowest $\delta$ means most shielded, think which $\text{CH}$ group is furthest from both the benzene ring and the electronegative nitrogen atom.
walkthrough:
Compare deshielding influences**
Nitrogen deshields adjacent protons c and e, moving them to higher $\delta$. The benzene ring deshields b. Proton f is the terminal $\text{CH}_{3}$ of the ethyl group, furthest from N and the ring, so it is most shielded.

Pick the lowest shift**
Alkyl $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{CH}_{2}$ only appears around $\delta$ 1. Therefore f has the lowest chemical shift.
